+# Package Audit — production_intelligence_brain (pre-v1.0.0 freeze)
+
+Audit date: 2026-09-17. Read-only investigation; no files inside
+`production_intelligence_brain/` were modified, moved, or deleted. This
+report is the only write produced.
+
+---
+
+## 1. Root-level duplicate CSVs
+
+Byte-for-byte comparison (`shasum`) of every root `MASTER_*.csv` against its
+`01_master_data/` counterpart:
+
+| File | Root sha1 | `01_master_data/` sha1 | Result |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| MASTER_ASSETS.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_AUDIO_EVENTS.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_AUDIO_VISUAL_SYNC.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_MOTIONS.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_SENTENCES.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_SHOTS.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_STATES.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+| MASTER_WORDS.csv | identical | identical | **IDENTICAL** |
+
+All 8 pairs are exact byte-for-byte duplicates. No divergence.
+
+**Reference grep** (all `.py`/`.md`/`.json` in the brain, for
+`MASTER_(ASSETS|AUDIO_EVENTS|AUDIO_VISUAL_SYNC|MOTIONS|SENTENCES|SHOTS|STATES|WORDS)\.csv`):
+every hit is a bare filename mention inside prose (docs describing "regenerated
+from `MASTER_X.csv`" etc.) or the validator's own source. None of the prose
+references carry a `01_master_data/` prefix nor a root/absolute-path prefix
+that would resolve to the root copies specifically — they are just filename
+mentions, not code paths, **except** `validator/validate_brain.py`, which is
+the only file that actually opens these CSVs programmatically:
+
+- `validator/validate_brain.py:19-20`: `BRAIN = dirname(dirname(abspath(__file__)))`; `MD = os.path.join(BRAIN, '01_master_data')`
+- `validator/validate_brain.py:30-33` (`load()`): opens `os.path.join(MD, name)` — i.e. always `01_master_data/<name>`, never the root.
+- `validator/validate_brain.py:44-51`: `load('MASTER_SENTENCES.csv')` etc. — all 8 loads go through `MD`.
+- `validator/validate_brain.py:381-382` (`CSV_FILES`) and `:384-386`: width-check loop also builds `path = os.path.join(MD, fname)` — `01_master_data/` only.
+- `validator/validate_brain.py:417-418`: the "canonical artifact presence" check requires the 8 files to exist at `BRAIN/01_master_data/<name>` — it does not check or reference the root copies at all.
+
+**Conclusion: nothing reads the root-level copies.** They are pure,
+unreferenced duplicates. Every consumer (validator, docs) resolves to
+`01_master_data/`. The root copies are dead weight for the v1.0.0 freeze —
+candidates for deletion (not performed here, per read-only mandate).
+
+---
+
+## 2. BRAIN_MANIFEST.json vs BRAIN_MANIFEST_VALIDATED.json
+
+`diff BRAIN_MANIFEST.json BRAIN_MANIFEST_VALIDATED.json` → **no output**
+(files are identical). `shasum` confirms: both
+`b162130056cf368a5ff78f86a02013e550cae92d`.
+
+Grep for `BRAIN_MANIFEST_VALIDATED` across the whole brain directory:
+**zero references anywhere** (not from `validate_brain.py`, not from any
+`.md`). Grep for `BRAIN_MANIFEST.json`: exactly one reference,
+`validator/validate_brain.py:439`, which lists it as one of the required
+top-level report files whose presence/non-triviality is checked.
+
+**Conclusion:** `BRAIN_MANIFEST_VALIDATED.json` is an untracked, unreferenced
+exact duplicate of `BRAIN_MANIFEST.json` — nothing points to it. Neither file
+is stale (see §7 — both match computed counts exactly); the issue is purely
+that `BRAIN_MANIFEST_VALIDATED.json` is a redundant, dangling copy that isn't
+part of the documented canonical contract.
+
+---
+
+## 3. DNA_INDEX.json staleness
+
+### Independently computed canonical counts (from `01_master_data/` and root `SOURCE_VIDEO_INDEX.csv`, verified two ways: manual `wc -l` row counts AND a full run of `validator/validate_brain.py`, which agree exactly)
+
+| Metric | Computed value |
+|---|---|
+| Source video count (`SOURCE_VIDEO_INDEX.csv` data rows) | **14** |
+| Word count (`MASTER_WORDS.csv`) | **7,864** |

+## 9. validator/validate_brain.py summary
+
+`validator/validate_brain.py` is a strict, from-disk integrity checker (no
+cached/remembered values — every number is computed at run time from the
+CSVs it loads). It performs, in order: (1) sentence validation — empty
+meaningful-sentence text, missing/invalid `FIRST_WORD_ID`/`LAST_WORD_ID`,
+`WORD_COUNT` vs actual linked-word count, negative sentence duration,
+duplicate `(VIDEO_SLUG, WORD_ID)` keys; (2) foreign-key checks for
+`MASTER_STATES`/`MASTER_SHOTS`'s `SHOT_ID`/`ASSET_IDS`/`MOTION_IDS`
+references; (3) A/V sync event validation — allowed
+`VISUAL_EVENT_TYPE`/`SYNC_RELATION` vocabularies, orphan
+`MOTION_ID(S)`/`SHOT_ID`/`TARGET_SHOT_ID`/`SOURCE_STATE`/`TARGET_STATE`/
+`SENTENCE_ID`/`WORD_ID`/`AUDIO_EVENT_ID` references, duplicate
+`(VIDEO_SLUG, SYNC_ID)`; (4) motion start/end linkage completeness (every
+motion has a `MOTION_START`; every non-instantaneous motion has a
+`MOTION_END`); (5) direct `MASTER_MOTIONS` validation — FK resolution,
+`DURATION_SEC` vs `END_SEC-START_SEC` arithmetic (±0.06s tolerance),
+duplicate IDs; (6) direct `MASTER_SHOTS`/`MASTER_STATES` validation — state
+duration arithmetic, state time-monotonicity within a shot, shot aggregate
+fields (`STATE_COUNT`/`MOTION_COUNT`/`FIRST_STATE_ID`/`LAST_STATE_ID`)
+recomputed and compared against stored values; (7) raw CSV width check (every
+row has the header's exact column count, catching unquoted-comma corruption
+`DictReader` would silently swallow); (8) a corpus-wide hard-timestamp rollup
+(`END_SEC < START_SEC` or unparseable); (9) canonical-artifact presence/
+non-triviality (>50 bytes) for the required file set; (10) a final row-count
+summary (echoed as the computed §3 numbers).
+
+**File paths it reads from:** exclusively `01_master_data/` — never the root
+copies. `BRAIN = dirname(dirname(abspath(__file__)))` and
+`MD = os.path.join(BRAIN, '01_master_data')` (lines 19-20); every `load()`
+call and the width-check loop resolve through `MD`. Confirmed by actually
+running it: `python3 validator/validate_brain.py` → `RESULT: PASS (all gates
+report zero failures)`, with the row-count summary matching §3 exactly. This
+directly answers §1: the validator is 01_master_data-only and would behave
+identically if the root duplicates were deleted.

@@ -0,0 +1,47 @@
+"""Run with python3; checks the saved forensic package without decoding again."""
+from pathlib import Path
+import csv,json,re
+R=Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
+def rows(p):return list(csv.DictReader((R/p).open()))
+def frame(t):
+ m,s=t.split(':');return round((int(m)*60+float(s))*24)
+t=rows('02_analysis/TIMELINE.csv');a=rows('02_analysis/ASSET_MANIFEST.csv');m=rows('02_analysis/MOTION_EVENTS.csv')
+states={x['STATE_ID']:x for x in t};assets={x['ASSET_ID'] for x in a};motions={x['MOTION_ID'] for x in m};shots=list(dict.fromkeys(x['SHOT_ID'] for x in t))
+assert len(states)==len(t) and len(assets)==len(a) and len(motions)==len(m)
+assert frame(t[0]['IN'])==0 and frame(t[-1]['OUT'])==2419
+for i,r in enumerate(t):
+ assert frame(r['IN'])<frame(r['OUT']),r
+ assert abs(float(r['DURATION'])-(frame(r['OUT'])-frame(r['IN']))/24)<0.00001
+ if i:assert r['IN']==t[i-1]['OUT'],r['STATE_ID']
+ assert set(r['ASSET_IDS'].split(';'))<=assets
+ assert set(filter(None,r['MOTION_IDS'].split(';')))<=motions
+ assert list((R/'01_evidence/frames').glob(f'f{frame(r["IN"]):04d}_*.png')),r['STATE_ID']
+valid={'SEQUENTIAL','SIMULTANEOUS_COUPLED','SIMULTANEOUS_INDEPENDENT','PERSISTENT_LOOP','CAMERA_SUBJECT_COUPLED','STATE_REPLACEMENT'}
+for r in m:
+ assert r['SOURCE_STATE'] in states and r['TARGET_STATE'] in states
+ assert states[r['SOURCE_STATE']]['SHOT_ID']==r['SHOT_ID']==states[r['TARGET_STATE']]['SHOT_ID']
+ assert r['RELATIONSHIP'] in valid and frame(r['IN'])<frame(r['OUT'])
+ assert frame(states[r['SOURCE_STATE']]['IN'])<=frame(r['IN'])
+ assert frame(states[r['TARGET_STATE']]['IN'])<frame(r['OUT'])
+ assert any(r['MOTION_ID'] in x['MOTION_IDS'].split(';') for x in t),r['MOTION_ID']
+ required=[x for x in t if x['SHOT_ID']==r['SHOT_ID']]
+ assert frame(required[0]['IN'])<=frame(r['IN'])<frame(r['OUT'])<=frame(required[-1]['OUT'])
+for p in ['03_capcut/CAPCUT_REBUILD.md','04_image_to_video/I2V_REBUILD.md']:
+ text=(R/p).read_text();assert re.findall(r'^## (S\d+) —',text,re.M)==shots
+cap=(R/'03_capcut/CAPCUT_REBUILD.md').read_text()
+for aid in motions:assert re.search(r'\b'+aid+r'\b',cap),aid
+anim=(R/'04_image_to_video/ANIMATION_PROMPTS.md').read_text()
+blocks=re.split(r'^## (A\d+)\n',anim,flags=re.M)[1:]
+assert set(blocks[0::2])==motions
+for aid,block in zip(blocks[0::2],blocks[1::2]):
+ p=block.split('ANIMATION PROMPT:\n',1)[1].strip();assert 0<len(p)<=500,(aid,len(p))
+images=(R/'04_image_to_video/IMAGE_PROMPTS.md').read_text();imgids=set(re.findall(r'^## (IMG\d+)$',images,re.M));assert len(imgids)==18
+assert images.count('TEXT BAKED: NO')==len(imgids)
+# Check relative Markdown links, including every indexed evidence frame.
+for p in R.rglob('*.md'):
+ for dest in re.findall(r'\]\(([^)]+)\)',p.read_text()):
+  if '://' not in dest and not dest.startswith('#'):
+   assert (p.parent/dest.split('#')[0]).exists(),(str(p),dest)
+metadata=json.loads((R/'00_source/metadata.json').read_text());assert len(metadata['streams'])==1 and metadata['streams'][0]['codec_type']=='video'
+run=json.loads((R/'RUN_STATE.json').read_text());expected={'shots':len(shots),'visual_states':len(t),'unique_assets':len(a),'motion_events':len(m),'unique_images':len(imgids),'audio_assets':0};assert run['counts']==expected
+print('PASS: timeline coverage, IDs, state evidence, both shot guides, all event recipes, prompt limits, file links, source stream facts and counts.')

+| Character DNA | Black circular/oval blank heads; stick limbs; no facial features, clothing detail or realistic skin. Held illustrated poses. | C03 headset and ponytail; C04 ponytail; C05 gray animal silhouette with eye/whiskers. Recurring graphic language does not prove character identity. |
+| Environment DNA | Off-white empty field, large negative space; isolated desks/diagrams. | S01 board inset; S11 dark treatment; S12 gray grainy field; S13 outdoor canopy/ground. |
+| Object DNA | Slightly irregular black contours; page-edge hatching, outlined devices, no photoreal surfaces. | Gray squirrel fill and solid black canopy; sparse scientific drawing texture. |
+| Color palette | Dominant off-white about #F7F7F7, near-black ink, restrained muted red about #BD4146. | Values APPROXIMATE from decoded RGB, not original swatches. S11 dark field approximately #2D2D2D; S12 gray near #CECECE. |
+| Lighting | Flat drawing with no changing cast shadows in most shots. | S11 six-frame darkening and six-frame recovery with soft stationary monitor light; S12 abrupt laptop light/rim appearance. |
+| Camera / framing | 9:16, locked perspective within all 13 shots. No evidenced pan, dolly, zoom or shake. | Changes in drawing scale happen at hard cuts, not camera animation. Angled book/paper art is part of the drawing. |
+| Composition | Clear isolated demonstration elements, approximate central/lower-middle scene placements, heavy use of top/bottom whitespace. | S04 intentionally crops page and keyboard; S11 words eventually fill field; S13 canopy fills upper-left. |
+| Typography | Hand-lettered uppercase with irregular stroke/baseline; little decoration; exact scientific units retained. | Original typeface UNKNOWN. Scientific page body is squiggles; book body is dense real lettering with clipped parts. Never invent missing words. |
+| Graphics | Small impact marks, curved explanatory leaders, red emphasis, word clouds, outlines and strike-throughs. | They communicate motion/typing but are often themselves completely still. |
+| Illustration / 3D style | Flat 2D black-ink diagram/cartoon drawing. | No evidence of 3D rendering or particular software/model. |
+| Depth | Overlap and local perspective in tables, books, keyboard and tree scene; no parallax. | No depth animation required. |
+| Motion language | Hard overlay onset, localized still replacement, text/mask reveals. Most running/typing/pain action is implied by held drawings. | S07 black lettering and red strokes sometimes overlap in time; S11 brightness fades. |
+| Transition language | 12 hard cuts; no crossfade between shots. Final frame holds to file end. | Fades are intra-shot lighting changes only. |
+| Asset reuse | Stationary base plate plus additive annotations; reused typist/desk visual vocabulary; density variants for TAP/CLICK; registered pose replacements. | LIKELY layered assembly is an efficient explanation; the flattened source cannot prove the original layer organization. |
+
+## Evidence and measurement conventions
+
+Frame numbers are authoritative at 24 fps; millisecond times are rounded. Coordinates throughout are normalized top-left percentages unless expressly given in source pixels. A source-aligned 1080×1920 full-frame overlay at 100% scale is the simplest exact registration. In CapCut a center-origin position of (0,0) corresponds to full-frame center; do not mistake normalized source coordinates for inspector units.
+
+A state can be a stable hold or a meaningful *reveal phase*. Continuous per-letter changes are grouped by word/line or strike, not inflated into hundreds of states. Motion endpoints may overlap the first complete-state frame. Instantaneous appearances occupy one frame in the motion map, followed by a hold in the timeline. Hard cuts are recorded in the timeline and are not counted again as object motion events.
+
+No full-video dense image dump was needed. All 2,419 frames were decoded for change screening; sparse full-duration visual review plus adjacent change-pair review and targeted dense S07/text/fade sampling establish the sequence. Compression-only changes on held plates were excluded. Microvariation below this sampling/codec resolution is not treated as an intentional effect.

+
+These are reusable source-image specifications, not claims that images have already been generated. Generate at 9:16/1080×1920 or a higher matching ratio, then register to the evidence. Text and diagram labels are not baked; source-derived overlays preserve exact wording. Reuse generated end frames only where the preceding state actually changes; never restart later actions from an unmodified base.

+## Continuity masters
+
+- CHARACTER: C02 uses blank oval head and simple stick limbs; retain scene-specific pose. C03 always keeps the same ponytail and headset shape. C04 remains a held running pose. No invented eyes/clothes or breathing.

+- OBJECT: retain desk/chair geometry, laptop angles, and measured book counts. Cables and socket panels are separate matched variants.
+- STYLE: 2D irregular black ink, white interiors, limited gray fill and muted-red annotations. Original font/software/model/source library UNKNOWN.

@@ -0,0 +1,13 @@
+# Audio map
+
+**OBSERVED:** ffprobe reports exactly one stream: H.264 video. The supplied MP4 has no audio track. This is a video-only source, not evidence that the original published work was intentionally silent.
+
+| Interval | Audio type | Supported description | Visual synchronization | Confidence |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| Entire source | NARRATION | Unavailable; no verified transcript supplied. | Spoken-word triggers cannot be assigned. | UNKNOWN |
+| Entire source | MUSIC | Unavailable. | No musical beat/cut matching can be verified. | UNKNOWN |
+| Entire source | SFX | Unavailable. Visible TAP/CLICK lettering is a graphic, not audible evidence. | Use visual A-ID onsets only. | UNKNOWN |
+| Entire source | AMBIENCE | Unavailable. | No ambience transition can be inferred. | UNKNOWN |
+| Entire source | SILENCE | Playback of this file produces no source sound because there is no audio stream. | Do not interpret this as an authored silence cue. | OBSERVED container fact; original intent UNKNOWN |
+
+There are **zero verified AU assets** and no fabricated audio events. Both build guides use an empty audio track to match this supplied file. If a matching audio-bearing reference later becomes available, inspect it, create persistent AU IDs and replace only SCRIPT_OR_AUDIO_CUE values with verified word/event timing. Existing frame timing remains the visual authority. Do not synthesize guessed narration, keyboard sounds, music or running footsteps.

+# Could you power your computer by typing?
+
+[00.000–03.980]
+
+"What would be the cumulative energy of hundreds of thousands of keystrokes required to write a novel?"
+
+[04.500–07.080]
+
+"There's a lot of engineering research into the force required to press keys,"
+
+[07.380–10.060]
+
+"in part because so many people suffer from repetitive strain injuries."
+
+[10.440–15.240]
+
+"Using data from a study of rubber dome keyboards, we can estimate that the energy required to press a key is around 1.5"
+
+[15.240–19.040]
+
+"milligules for a letter key and 2.5 for a big key like enterer or spacebar."
+
+[19.400–23.780]
+
+"How much is 1.5 milligules? Well, it's enough to heat a drop of water by 1% of a degree."
+
+[24.160–28.760]
+
+"It's also enough to lift a squirrel 300 microns all the way from the ground to the top of a stack of"
+
+[28.760–32.880]
+
+"four sheets of paper. A typical novel might have half a million to a million characters in it,"
+
+[33.020–35.360]
+
+"so typing it out would require at least that many key presses."
+
+[35.920–39.000]
+
+"The amount of backspacing and rewriting varies wildly from person to person."
+
+[39.260–42.600]
+
+"Some people write straight through without pausing or editing while others re-rate every sentence"
+
+[42.600–45.980]
+
+"endlessly. It turns on not to make a big difference which kind of writer you are."
+
+[46.260–48.960]
+
+"If you write straight through without editing, you'd expend about a killigule."
+
+[49.280–51.620]
+
+"With a lot of re-writes, you might expend several killigules,"
+
+[51.780–56.420]
+
+"but you'd need to re-write every word 10 times to match the energy stored in a single AA battery."
+
+[56.420–61.640]
+
+"Writing one full novel would provide an off-energy to run a laptop for a total of about 30 seconds."
+
+[61.940–65.740]
+
+"If each novel takes you six months, you'd spend two seconds out of every million running off"
+
+[65.740–70.320]
+
+"keyboard power. A novel every six months seems like a lot of typing, but plenty of people type more."
+
+[70.640–74.380]
+
+"If you abandon the requirement of writing actual words and just care about the most key presses,"
+
+[74.760–79.960]
+
+"eSports is a promising place to look. Top eSports professionals can clock in over 400 actions per minute,"
+
+[80.100–83.160]
+
+"which are a mix of mouse clicks and keystrokes. Taking a conservative estimate,"
+
+[83.160–86.780]
+
+"a top eSports player types the equivalent of a novel in a few days of playing time."
+
+[87.300–90.820]
+
+"However, a few days still isn't fast enough to represent much energy."
+
+[91.220–95.420]
+
+"Remember to keep a laptop running from key press power alone, you'd need to write a novel in half a minute."
+
+[95.740–99.300]
+
+"Even for the fastest typists, writing is not a novel form of exercise."
+

+# Video forensic reconstruction — videoplayback
+
+## Source summary
+
+[videoplayback.mp4 manifest](00_source/SOURCE_MANIFEST.md): 100.791667 seconds, 1080×1920, 9:16, 24 fps, 2,419 frames, H.264. No audio stream.
+
+## Observed production DNA
+
+See [VISUAL_DNA.md](02_analysis/VISUAL_DNA.md) for the evidence-supported drawing, color, typography and motion rules. The source uses held ink illustrations, additive graphics, localized state replacements and short reveals; all shots have locked framing.
+
+## Counts
+
+| Measure | Count |
+|---|---:|
+| Shots | 13 |
+| Meaningful visual states, including reveal endpoints/phases | 97 |
+| Unique production asset IDs, variants grouped | 40 |
+| Intra-shot motion/change events, excluding hard cuts | 59 |
+| Required unique source image prompts | 18 |
+| Verified audio assets | 0 |
+
+## WAY 1 — CapCut overview
+
+[LIMITED — CapCut build guide](03_capcut/CAPCUT_REBUILD.md). Every shot and A-ID has a layer/edit recipe. Source-aligned stills and exact graphic overlays are the closest route to the observed pixels. Limitations below apply.
+
+## WAY 2 — Image-to-video overview
+
+[LIMITED — I2V build guide](04_image_to_video/I2V_REBUILD.md). Reuse generated masters; hold static scenes; composite exact labels, masks and abrupt changes. Animation prompts cover observed changes without authorizing invented motion. Limitations below apply.
+
+## Important fidelity limitations
+
+- The supplied file has no audio stream. Narration/music/SFX and spoken synchronization remain UNKNOWN; both workflows reproduce the supplied silent playback only.
+- Original source layers, font, software/model and asset provenance are UNKNOWN. Source-derived/traced stills can match visible geometry; freshly generated linework/font/objects are approximate.
+- Tiny scientific-body marks are not readable prose; portions of book text and calendar dates are clipped/too small for certain transcription. Preserve the source artwork rather than invent wording.
+- Mask paths and soft light falloff are measured visual approximations; original easing/effect values cannot be recovered. Frame onsets are measured; first faint pixels of reveals can differ by about one frame.
+- This deliverable is the analysis, evidence and independently usable reconstruction specifications. It does not include a native CapCut project, generated image/video assets or an exported rebuilt video.
+

+# Visual DNA
+
+## Observed global rules
+
+- **Characters:** black, loose hand-drawn stick figures; circles for heads; no filled skin or clothing. Character scale changes only with composition changes.
+- **Environments/objects:** white paper-like field with thin black line drawings. Cave scenes add ice overhangs, snow ground, and sparse dots. Scientific inserts use crisp diagrams, whiteboards, black field, or light gray sun-edge gradient.
+- **Palette/lighting:** near-white ground, black lines, dark charcoal backgrounds, and sparse signal red annotations. A soft gray-white edge glow appears only in Sun/heat inserts.
+- **Camera/composition:** locked full-frame 16:9 compositions. Cuts or panel replacement create most changes; no evidence of decorative camera drift, parallax, or depth of field.
+- **Typography/graphics:** hand-lettered all-caps display labels and thin technical text. Exact words should be added as editor text where legibility matters. Red arrows, red “BAD” labels, and red crossed-out values are semantic emphasis.
+- **Motion language:** drawings appear through short holds, hard cuts, panel swaps, simple translation, and incremental write-on/reveal states. Static drawings stay static after arrival.
+- **Transition language:** hard cuts predominate. S03/S13 use a three-panel or doorway composition; S08 deliberately alternates black and white panels. S02/S14 are red identity/end cards.
+- **Asset reuse:** C01 lecturer and E01 board recur; E02 cave and C02 explorer recur at opening and close. The Sun-edge gradient and C03 silhouette recur in comparison/exposure inserts.
+
+## Scene-specific exceptions
+
+- S02 and S14 replace monochrome illustration with solid red branded card.
+- S08 alternates high-contrast black/gray and white technical panels; preserve cuts rather than blending them.
+- S11 adds anatomical X-ray-like line art and a red warning placard to otherwise whiteboard staging.

+[00.000–02.120]
+
+"This question comes from AJ, who wrote,"
+
+[02.420–03.340]
+
+"When I was about 8 years old,"
+
+[03.440–05.020]
+
+"shoveling snow on a freezing day in Colorado,"
+
+[05.440–08.240]
+
+"I wish that I could instantly be transported to the surface of the sun,"
+
+[08.480–10.660]
+
+"just for a nanosecond and then instantly transported back."
+
+[11.060–13.800]
+
+"I figured this would be long enough to warm me up, but not enough to harm me."
+
+[14.200–15.020]
+
+"What would actually happen?"
+
+[17.120–19.200]
+
+"Believe it or not, this wouldn't even warm you."
+
+[19.520–22.420]
+
+"The temperature of the surface of the sun is about 5,800K, give or take."
+
+[22.720–24.880]
+
+"If you stayed there for a while, you'd be cooked to a sender."
+
+[25.080–26.640]
+
+"But a nanosecond is not very long."
+
+[26.920–28.960]
+
+"It's enough time for light to travel about a foot."
+
+[29.480–31.060]
+
+"I'm going to assume you're facing toward the sun."
+
+[31.320–33.520]
+
+"In general, you should avoid looking directly at the sun,"
+
+[33.660–36.860]
+
+"but it's hard to avoid when it takes up to full 180 degrees of your view."
+
+[37.340–40.100]
+
+"In that nanosecond, about a microjoule of energy would enter your eye."
+
+[40.520–42.100]
+
+"A microjoule of light is not a lot."
+
+[42.340–44.060]
+
+"If you start a computer monitor with your eyes closed,"
+
+[44.260–46.060]
+
+"and then you open them and shut them very quickly,"
+
+[46.360–49.200]
+
+"your eye will take in about as much light from the screen during your reverse blink"
+
+[49.200–51.280]
+
+"as it would during a nanosecond on the sun's surface."
+
+[51.680–52.440]
+
+"Is there a word for that?"
+
+[52.660–54.200]
+
+"Like a blink, but in reverse?"
+
+[54.640–55.840]
+
+"I feel like there should be a word for that."
+
+[56.200–58.160]
+
+"Anyway, during the nanosecond on the sun,"
+
+[58.160–61.200]
+
+"photons from the sun would float into your eye and strike your retinal cells."
+
+[61.520–63.920]
+
+"Then, at the end of the nanosecond, you'd jump back home."
+
+[64.280–66.800]
+
+"At this point, the retinal cells wouldn't have even begun responding."
+
+[67.160–69.740]
+
+"Over the next few million nanoseconds, or milliseconds,"
+
+[70.280–72.560]
+
+"the retinal cells, having absorbed a bunch of light energy,"
+
+[72.900–75.680]
+
+"would get into gear and start signaling to your brain that something had happened."
+
+[76.160–77.800]
+
+"You would spend one nanosecond on the sun,"
+
+[78.000–80.680]
+
+"but it would take 30 million nanoseconds for your brain to notice."
+
+[81.200–83.060]
+
+"From your point of view, all you would see is a flash."
+
+[83.420–85.800]
+
+"The flash would seem to last much longer than your time on the sun,"
+
+[85.800–88.520]
+
+"only fading as your retinal cells finally quieted down."
+
+[89.000–90.780]
+
+"The energy absorbed by your skin would be minor,"
+
+[91.020–94.120]
+
+"about 10 to the minus 5 joules per square centimeter of exposed skin."
+
+[94.580–97.660]
+
+"To compare a sin, according to the IEEE P1584 standard,"
+
+[97.940–100.620]
+
+"holding your finger in the blue flame of a butane lighter for one second"
+
+[100.620–103.240]
+
+"delivers about 5 joules per square centimeter to the skin,"
+
+[103.500–105.980]
+
+"which is roughly the threshold for receiving a second degree burn."
+
+[106.500–109.700]
+
+"The heat during your sun visit would be 5 orders of magnitude weaker than that."
+
+[110.020–112.860]
+
+"So, other than the dim flash in your eyes, you might not even notice."
+
+[113.340–115.000]
+
+"But what if you got the coordinates wrong?"
+
+[115.520–117.320]
+
+"The sun's surface is relatively cool."
+
+[117.760–119.080]
+
+"It's hotter than like Phoenix,"
+
+[119.380–121.820]
+
+"but compared to the interior of the sun, it's downright chilly."
+
+[122.320–123.640]
+
+"The surface is a few thousand degrees,"
+
+[123.840–125.720]
+
+"but the interior is a few million degrees."
+
+[126.120–127.580]
+
+"What if you spend a nanosecond there?"
+
+[128.120–130.700]
+
+"This defon Boltzmann law lets us calculate how much heat you'd absorb"
+
+[130.700–131.680]
+
+"well inside the sun."
+
+[132.040–132.600]
+
+"It's not good."
+
+[133.000–136.400]
+
+"You would exceed the IEEE P1584B standard for second-degree burns"
+
+[136.400–138.240]
+
+"after one femtosecond in the sun."
+
+[138.580–141.820]
+
+"A nanosecond, the time you're spending there, is a million femtoseconds."
+
+[142.160–143.240]
+
+"This doesn't end well for you."
+
+[143.560–144.480]
+
+"But there's some good news."
+
+[144.480–146.480]
+
+"Deep in the sun, the photon's carrying energy"
+
+[146.480–147.760]
+
+"around have very short wavelengths."
+
+[148.220–151.820]
+
+"They're not visible light, they're mostly a mix of what we consider hard and soft x-rays."
+
+[152.220–154.600]
+
+"This means that they penetrate into your body to various depths,"
+
+[154.880–157.240]
+
+"heating your internal organs, and also ionizing your DNA,"
+
+[157.600–160.080]
+
+"causing irreversible damage before they even start burning you."
+
+[160.400–163.220]
+
+"Looking back, I realized I started that by saying there's some good news."
+
+[163.620–164.360]
+
+"I don't know why I did that."
+
+[164.700–166.200]
+
+"Don't spend a nanosecond inside the sun."
+
+[166.680–168.980]
+
+"In Greek legend, Icarus flew too close to the sun,"
+
+[169.180–171.140]
+
+"and the heat melded his wings and he fell to his death."
+
+[171.560–174.060]
+
+"It's true that the temperature is higher closer to the sun,"
+
+[174.060–176.120]
+
+"but temperature and heat aren't the same thing."
+
+[176.560–178.640]
+
+"Melting, or any phase change of a substance,"
+
+[178.920–182.060]
+
+"requires the absorption of a specific amount of heat energy per kilogram,"
+
+[182.480–186.620]
+
+"and the heat absorbed is a function of both the temperature and the length of time you're exposed to it,"
+
+[186.800–188.140]
+
+"which brings us back to Icarus."
+
+[188.480–190.960]
+
+"His wings didn't melt because he flew too close to the sun."
+
+[191.300–193.020]
+
+"They melted because he spent too much time there."
+
+[193.720–196.380]
+
+"Visit briefly in Little Hops, and you can go anywhere."
+
+[207.140–208.540]
+
+"Visit briefly in Little Hops, and you can go anywhere."

+could_you_survive_nanosecond_sun,S0041,103.5,105.98,which is roughly the threshold for receiving a second degree burn.,,,11,,
+could_you_survive_nanosecond_sun,S0042,106.5,109.7,The heat during your sun visit would be 5 orders of magnitude weaker than that.,,,15,,
+could_you_survive_nanosecond_sun,S0043,110.02,112.86,"So, other than the dim flash in your eyes, you might not even notice.",,,14,,

+could_you_survive_nanosecond_sun,S0050,126.12,127.58,What if you spend a nanosecond there?,,,7,,

+# VISUAL DNA
+
+Global, evidence-supported production characteristics. Scene-specific detail lives in TIMELINE.csv / ASSET_MANIFEST.csv — not repeated here.
+
+## ENVIRONMENT DNA
+- Flat solid white/off-white canvas for the entire video (OBSERVED). No background photography, no gradients, no depth layers.
+- No camera moves, no parallax, no depth-of-field anywhere (OBSERVED — zero scene cuts detected, all "cuts" are 2D layer swaps on the same flat canvas).
+
+## CHARACTER DNA
+- One recurring minimalist stick-figure design (circle head, straight-line limbs, no facial detail beyond dot eyes) reused across 4 poses/props (interview duo, NASA-badge figure, distressed figure, headset figure). See C01.
+
+## OBJECT / ILLUSTRATION DNA
+- Uniform hand-drawn / sketch line-art style for every illustration (seismograph, newspaper, globe, fault-block slabs, debris) — black ink linework, thin uniform stroke weight, minimal or flat grey shading, no gradients or 3D rendering (OBSERVED).
+- Central recurring visual metaphor: a grey globe/Earth icon that accumulates visible "damage" states as the fictional magnitude escalates (clean → epicenter marks → cracked → spiky border → exploded debris). This is the emotional/visual throughline of the whole piece (OBSERVED progression, LIKELY intentional escalation device).
+- Red ink is reserved exclusively for "alert/annotation" marks: strike-throughs, circles, epicenter ripples, the climbing scribble — never used for the base illustrations (OBSERVED, consistent rule across the whole video).
+
+## COLOR PALETTE
+- Background: white/off-white (#FFFFFF-ish).
+- Line art: black.
+- Fills: flat light-to-mid grey (globe, slabs).
+- Accent: red (annotations, alerts, epicenters, "danger" scribbles) — the only saturated color used anywhere in the video (OBSERVED).
+
+## TYPOGRAPHY (T01/T02)
+- T01 (titles): bold, all-caps, hand-drawn/marker-style sans-serif, large, centered top of canvas.
+- T02 (captions/annotations): same type family, much smaller, regular weight, used for facts, dates, measurements, and punchlines.
+- No other type styles appear anywhere in the video (OBSERVED).
+
+## GRAPHICS / UI LANGUAGE
+- E02 (the vertical ruler/number-line) is the single persistent HUD element from F01.5 onward — it never fully disappears once introduced, acting as a constant visual reminder of "where we are on the scale" (OBSERVED).
+- G01 ("LIVE" broadcast box) is a reusable template appearing 3 times with different internal content — the video's go-to device for a punchline/reaction beat (OBSERVED reuse pattern).
+
+## COMPOSITION
+- Every state is centered, single-column, vertically stacked (title → illustration → optional caption/box), consistent with 9:16 short-form framing (OBSERVED).
+
+## MOTION LANGUAGE
+- No camera motion anywhere. All motion is 2D layer animation: fade-ins, one draw-on (strike-through, circle), one continuous scale-up (the ruler, once), and hard cuts between major "screens" (OBSERVED — see MOTION_EVENTS.csv).
+- Hard cuts are used specifically at every full-topic change (new magnitude number); fades/draw-ons are used for additions *within* a topic. This is a consistent authorial rule (LIKELY intentional pacing device).
+
+## TRANSITION LANGUAGE
+- Two transition types only: (1) instant hard cut (STATE_REPLACEMENT, used ~11 times at major beats) and (2) opacity fade-in (used for additive annotations within a state). No wipes, no slides, no 3D transitions anywhere (OBSERVED).
+
+## ASSET REUSE PATTERN
+- High reuse of structural templates (G01 LIVE box x3, C01 stick figure x4 poses, E02 ruler throughout, E03 globe across 4 damage states) vs. single-use "punchline" illustrations (E01 seismograph, O01 newspaper, O02 phone, O03 fault-blocks) that appear exactly once each. This 80/20 pattern (few reusable structural assets + many disposable gag assets) is the core efficiency pattern of the production (OBSERVED).
+
+## FIDELITY LIMITATION
+- Sub-0.5-second easing curves (exact fade durations, exact scale-up curve of the ruler, exact rotation speed of the globe) cannot be measured precisely from 2fps sampling; all such values are marked APPROXIMATE or LIKELY in MOTION_EVENTS.csv rather than fabricated as exact numbers.

+"A magnitude 9 earthquake already measurably alters the rotation of the Earth."
+
+[21.520–24.980]
+
+"The two magnitude 9 plus earthquakes this century both altered the length of the day"
+
+[24.980–26.940]
+
+"by a tiny but measurable fraction of a second."
+
+[26.940–31.780]
+
+"In order to get to magnitude 10, you'd need a ruptured fault line 3.5,000 kilometers long,"
+
+[32.180–35.480]
+
+"and a magnitude 11 quake would require a fault that went halfway around the world."
+
+[35.860–39.320]
+
+"A magnitude 15 earthquake would be a million times more powerful than that,"
+
+[39.520–42.500]
+
+"and involve the release of enough energy to evaporate all the water on Earth."
+
+[42.820–46.040]
+
+"Though if that happened, we could rest easy knowing the earthquake couldn't cause any tsunamis."
+
+[46.560–50.840]
+
+"Going a few steps further, a magnitude 18 earthquake would release nearly 10 to the 32"
+
+[50.840–54.320]
+
+"jewels of energy, which is roughly the gravitational binding energy of the Earth."
+
+[54.320–58.360]
+
+"To put it another way, the Death Star caused a magnitude 18 earthquake on Alderron."
+
+[58.740–61.480]
+
+"You could in theory talk about a more powerful earthquake on Earth,"
+
+[61.680–65.600]
+
+"but in practice all it would mean is that the expanding cloud of space debris would be faster and hotter."
+

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Self-contained validator for how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset.
+Run: python3 00_source/verify.py   (from this video's project root)
+Stdlib only. Prints PASS or raises AssertionError on the first failure.
+"""
+import csv
+import json
+import re
+from pathlib import Path
+
+ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
+
+def read_csv(name):
+    with open(ROOT / "02_analysis" / name, newline="") as f:
+        return list(csv.DictReader(f))
+
+def read_text(rel):
+    return (ROOT / rel).read_text()
+
+# ---- Timeline coverage ----
+timeline = read_csv("TIMELINE.csv")
+assert len(timeline) == 48, f"expected 48 states, got {len(timeline)}"
+rows = sorted(timeline, key=lambda r: int(r["IN"]))
+expected_in = 0
+total_frames = 0
+for r in rows:
+    in_f, out_f = int(r["IN"]), int(r["OUT"])
+    assert in_f == expected_in, f"gap/overlap before state {r['STATE_ID']}: expected IN={expected_in}, got {in_f}"
+    assert out_f >= in_f, f"invalid range in state {r['STATE_ID']}"
+    dur_frames = int(r["DURATION"].split("/")[0])
+    assert dur_frames == out_f - in_f + 1, f"duration mismatch in state {r['STATE_ID']}"
+    expected_in = out_f + 1
+    total_frames += dur_frames
+assert total_frames == 3117, f"total frames {total_frames} != 3117"
+assert rows[-1]["OUT"] == "3116", "timeline does not reach the last frame (3116)"
+
+shots = sorted(set(r["SHOT_ID"] for r in timeline), key=lambda s: int(s[1:]))
+assert shots == [f"S{n:02d}" for n in range(1, 15)], f"unexpected shot set: {shots}"
+
+# ---- Asset manifest ----
+assets = read_csv("ASSET_MANIFEST.csv")
+assert len(assets) == 29, f"expected 29 assets, got {len(assets)}"
+asset_ids = set(a["ASSET_ID"] for a in assets)
+assert len(asset_ids) == 29, "duplicate ASSET_ID found"
+
+def split_ids(s):
+    return [x.strip() for x in s.split(";") if x.strip()]
+
+referenced_assets = set()
+for r in timeline:
+    referenced_assets |= set(split_ids(r["ASSET_IDS"]))
+missing = referenced_assets - asset_ids
+assert not missing, f"TIMELINE references unknown asset IDs: {missing}"
+
+# ---- Motion events ----
+motions = read_csv("MOTION_EVENTS.csv")
+assert len(motions) == 34, f"expected 34 motion events, got {len(motions)}"
+motion_ids = set(m["MOTION_ID"] for m in motions)
+assert motion_ids == {f"A{n:02d}" for n in range(1, 35)}, f"unexpected motion ID set: {sorted(motion_ids)}"
+for m in motions:
+    assert m["SHOT_ID"] in shots, f"motion {m['MOTION_ID']} references unknown shot {m['SHOT_ID']}"
+    assert int(m["OUT"]) >= int(m["IN"]), f"motion {m['MOTION_ID']} has invalid IN/OUT"
+
+referenced_motions = set()
+for r in timeline:
+    for mid in split_ids(r["MOTION_IDS"]):
+        if mid.startswith("A") and mid[1:].isdigit():
+            referenced_motions.add(mid)
+missing_m = referenced_motions - motion_ids
+assert not missing_m, f"TIMELINE references unknown motion IDs: {missing_m}"
+
+# ---- CapCut guide ----
+capcut = read_text("03_capcut/CAPCUT_REBUILD.md")
+for s in shots:
+    assert re.search(rf"^## {s} ", capcut, re.M), f"CAPCUT_REBUILD.md missing header for {s}"
+for mid in sorted(motion_ids):
+    assert mid in capcut, f"CAPCUT_REBUILD.md never references motion {mid}"
+
+# ---- Image prompts ----
+img_prompts = read_text("04_image_to_video/IMAGE_PROMPTS.md")
+img_headers = re.findall(r"^## (IMG\d+)$", img_prompts, re.M)
+assert len(img_headers) == 14, f"expected 14 IMG headers, got {len(img_headers)}"
+assert img_headers == [f"IMG{n:02d}" for n in range(1, 15)], f"unexpected/non-sequential IMG headers: {img_headers}"
+assert img_prompts.count("TEXT BAKED: NO") == 13, "expected 13 standalone image prompts declaring TEXT BAKED: NO (IMG14 is a reuse stub with no prompt of its own)"
+
+# ---- Animation prompts ----
+anim = read_text("04_image_to_video/ANIMATION_PROMPTS.md")
+anim_headers = re.findall(r"^## (A\d+)$", anim, re.M)
+assert set(anim_headers) == motion_ids, f"ANIMATION_PROMPTS.md headers {sorted(anim_headers)} != motion set {sorted(motion_ids)}"
+for block in re.split(r"^## A\d+$", anim, flags=re.M)[1:]:
+    m = re.search(r"ANIMATION PROMPT:\s*(.+?)(?:\n##|\Z)", block, re.S)
+    assert m, "a motion block is missing its ANIMATION PROMPT line"
+    prompt_text = m.group(1).strip()
+    assert 1 <= len(prompt_text) <= 500, f"animation prompt out of 1-500 char range ({len(prompt_text)} chars)"
+
+# ---- I2V guide ----
+i2v = read_text("04_image_to_video/I2V_REBUILD.md")
+for s in shots:
+    assert re.search(rf"^## {s} ", i2v, re.M), f"I2V_REBUILD.md missing header for {s}"
+
+# ---- Audio map sanity ----
+audio_map = read_text("05_audio/AUDIO_MAP.md")
+assert "UNAVAILABLE" in audio_map, "AUDIO_MAP.md should record that transcript is unavailable"
+assert "25.06" in audio_map, "AUDIO_MAP.md missing first measured silence gap"
+
+# ---- Cross-project markdown link check ----
+link_re = re.compile(r"\[[^\]]*\]\(([^)]+)\)")
+for md_file in ROOT.rglob("*.md"):
+    text = md_file.read_text(errors="ignore")
+    for target in link_re.findall(text):
+        if target.startswith("http") or target.startswith("#"):
+            continue
+        target_path = (md_file.parent / target.split("#")[0]).resolve()
+        assert target_path.exists(), f"{md_file.relative_to(ROOT)} has a broken link to {target}"
+
+# ---- RUN_STATE.json counts (if present and populated) ----
+run_state_path = ROOT / "RUN_STATE.json"
+if run_state_path.exists():
+    run_state = json.loads(run_state_path.read_text())
+    counts = run_state.get("counts")
+    if counts:
+        assert counts["shots"] == 14
+        assert counts["visual_states"] == 48
+        assert counts["unique_assets"] == 29
+        assert counts["motion_events"] == 34
+        assert counts["unique_images"] == 14
+
+print("PASS: timeline coverage, asset/motion ID cross-refs, CapCut shot+motion coverage, "
+      "image/animation prompt counts and length limits, I2V shot coverage, audio map sanity, "
+      "and file links.")

+# Visual DNA — how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset
+
+Global, evidence-supported production characteristics. Scene-specific detail lives in `TIMELINE.csv`/`ASSET_MANIFEST.csv`; this file states only repeated rules and their exceptions.
+
+## CHARACTER DNA
+- Repeated rule: humans are rendered as minimal stick figures — a plain circle head with no facial features and thin line limbs (C01), used identically as a reader, desk-worker, and pedestrian.
+- Exceptions or limits: the camera-crew pair (C02) is a distinct, more detailed silhouette design (visible hair, tripod camera prop) reserved only for the two photographic-style sunset shots (S03, S14); it never appears in the flat-diagram shots.
+
+## ENVIRONMENT DNA
+- Repeated rule: two visually distinct backdrop families recur — (1) a plain white canvas for schematic/diagram shots, and (2) painterly gradient-sky backdrops for "real-world" location shots (E02 polar dusk, E07 ocean sunset).
+- Exceptions or limits: E01 (chalkboard) and E05 (office desk) and E06 (church) are unique single-shot environments that don't recur or blend with the two main families.
+
+## OBJECT DNA
+- Repeated rule: the sun/shadow relationship is always drawn as a small flat yellow circle (G01) paired with a small flat grey circle (G02), regardless of which larger diagram it appears in (horizon chains, mountain rolls, recap insets, map legends).
+- Exceptions or limits: in the two full-scale "real" location shots (S07, S08) and the two photographic sunset shots (S03, S14), the sun is instead rendered as a larger illustrated/painterly disc, not the small flat schematic circle.
+
+## COLOR PALETTE
+- Repeated rule: diagram shots use a restricted grey/black/white/yellow palette (white canvas, black line art, yellow sun accents, grey shadow accents), with red reserved exclusively for rejection marks (X), directional arrows, and callout labels.
+- Exceptions or limits: the two photographic sunset shots (S03, S14) and the two polar establishing shots (S07, S08) use a full painterly gradient palette (deep blue/purple night sky through red-orange-yellow sunset colors) that departs from the flat diagram palette.
+
+## LIGHTING
+- Repeated rule: diagram shots are flat and shadeless (no rendered light source other than labeled sun/shadow icons).
+- Exceptions or limits: the photographic/painterly shots (S03, S07, S08, S14) simulate directional light via gradient skies and a glowing sun disc with a water/ice reflection.
+
+## CAMERA / FRAMING
+- Repeated rule: every shot in this video uses a static, locked camera — OBSERVED across all 14 shots; no pans, zooms, or tracking moves were detected anywhere in the source.
+- Exceptions or limits: none observed. (The apparent "movement" in several shots — cars, sun circles, terminator arrows — is graphic-element motion within a fixed frame, not camera motion.)
+
+## COMPOSITION
+- Repeated rule: diagram shots are built around a single dominant horizontal reference line (a horizon line, a globe terminator, or a map's day/night band) with graphic elements arranged along or around it.
+- Exceptions or limits: the chalkboard shot (S01) and photographic shots (S03/S14) are composed as full-bleed single-subject frames rather than around a horizontal reference line.
+
+## TYPOGRAPHY
+- Repeated rule: all on-screen text is a single consistent white, hand-lettered/rounded sans-serif caption style, used for location labels, data callouts, and dialogue.
+- Exceptions or limits: none observed — caption styling is uniform across all shots that carry text (S03, S05-S14).
+
+## GRAPHICS
+- Repeated rule: rejection/confirmation is always communicated with a red hand-drawn X (wrong) or green check mark (right), never with color grading, sound stingers alone, or a spoken-only "no."
+- Exceptions or limits: none observed.
+
+## ILLUSTRATION / 3D STYLE
+- Repeated rule: flat 2D vector/line-art illustration dominates (chalkboard, all circle/horizon diagrams, map shots, desk/church shots).
+- Exceptions or limits: S06 uses a pseudo-3D wireframe/graticule globe render (grid lines suggesting a sphere in perspective) — the only shot with any implied 3D depth; S03/S07/S08/S14 use painterly/gradient rendering rather than flat vector fills.
+
+## DEPTH
+- Repeated rule: diagram shots are single-plane (foreground graphics directly on a flat background, no midground layer).
+- Exceptions or limits: the photographic sunset and polar-location shots (S03, S07, S08, S14) use a simple foreground/background depth split (silhouette figures or vehicles in front of a gradient sky/horizon).
+
+## MOTION LANGUAGE
+- Repeated rule: nearly all motion in this video is graphic-element reveal/build (objects, arrows, and captions being progressively drawn onto an otherwise static frame) rather than continuous physical animation; OBSERVED across S02, S04-S06, S08-S14.
+- Exceptions or limits: S01's globe spin, S04's mountain-roll gag, and S10/S12's car-advancing-along-a-path are the only cases of an element continuously translating/rotating rather than simply appearing.
+
+## TRANSITION LANGUAGE
+- Repeated rule: shot changes are hard cuts (OBSERVED via the `ffmpeg` scene-change filter for 11 of the 13 inter-shot boundaries).
+- Exceptions or limits: two boundaries (S07→S08 and S13→S14) were not flagged by the automated scene-change detector despite a clear visual content change; these are labeled LIKELY DISSOLVE / LIKELY CUT respectively in `TIMELINE.csv` based on direct frame comparison rather than the detector.
+
+## ASSET REUSE PATTERN
+- Repeated rule: the small schematic sun/shadow circle pair (G01/G02) and the horizon-line motif (G03) are the throughline connecting nearly every diagram shot (S02, S04, S09, S10, S12, S13); the video's two "bookend" photographic sunset shots (S03, S14) reuse the exact same background plate (E07) and character pair (C02).
+- Exceptions or limits: the North Pole (S07) and Longyearbyen (S08) establishing shots share a sky-gradient language (E02) but do NOT share foreground assets — each has its own unique vehicle and background silhouette.
+
+## Evidence and measurement conventions
+- All timing is expressed in frames at the source's true constant frame rate: 24fps, 3117 total frames, 129.875s video duration.
+- Shot/state boundaries were established primarily from 130 source-resolution 1fps frame extractions, cross-checked against `ffmpeg` scene-change detection at thresholds 0.25 and 0.10. Two shot boundaries were not confirmed by the automated detector (see Transition Language above) and are marked LIKELY rather than OBSERVED for their exact frame-level cut point; all other boundaries are OBSERVED at 1-second precision.
+- Long/continuous motions (A09 mountain roll, A24 car-and-legend advance) were confirmed smooth and single-direction via 1s interval sampling, not exhaustive native-frame verification; their internal easing/pacing is LIKELY steady rather than confirmed exact.

+"I ran a search for a long sunset driving path using some Pi FM code and GPS traces of"
+
+[99.920–103.880]
+
+"Norwegian highways, and I found that the strategy works about equally well anywhere inside the Arctic"
+
+[103.880–108.280]
+
+"Circle. Over a wide range of routes and driving speeds, the longest sunset I could come up with was"
+
+[108.280–112.420]
+
+"consistently about 95 minutes, which is about 40 minutes longer than the longest sunset you can get"
+
+[112.420–116.620]
+
+"in Long-Year Bien. But if you are stuck on Svalbard and you want to make the sunset or sunrise,"
+
+[116.620–120.920]
+
+"less a little longer, you can always try spinning counterclockwise, so your angular momentum"
+
+[120.920–125.720]
+
+"slows the Earth's rotation. It's true that it will only add an imperceptibly small fraction of"
+
+[125.720–127.940]
+
+"a nanosecond, but it might be worth it."

+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0000,0.0,2.88,"What's the longest possible sunset you can experience while driving,",,,10,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0001,3.08,5.34,assuming you're obeying the speed limit and driving on paved roads?,,,11,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0002,5.8,9.2,"For the purpose of our question, sunset starts the instant the sun touches the horizon",,,15,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0003,9.2,13.32,"and ends when it disappears completely, which means that for us, this is not a sunset.",,,16,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0004,13.82,17.22,This is also not a sunset. This is definitely not a sunset.,,,12,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0005,17.64,20.5,"And no matter what happens here, this will not be a sunset.",,,12,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0006,21.04,24.64,"If the sun touches the horizon and then it lifts back up, the sunset is disqualified.",,,16,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0007,25.34,28.86,"For a sunset to count, the sun also can't just disappear behind a nearby hill.",,,15,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0008,28.86,31.14,It needs to set behind the ideal horizon.,,,8,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0009,31.5,35.54,"At London's latitude, the Earth's surface is moving from west to east at about a thousand kilometers per hour.",,,19,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0010,35.82,39.32,"So if you fly west in a commercial airliner, you can experience an arbitrarily long sunset,",,,16,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0011,39.64,42.54,or at least you can tell you run at a fuel 15 or 20 hours in.,,,16,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0012,43.04,46.56,"Intuitively, it seems like we probably want to be as far north or maybe south as possible.",,,17,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0013,46.86,49.4,"The closer we are to the pole, the easier it is to keep up with the sun.",,,17,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0014,50.06,52.88,"Unfortunately, there are no paved roads anywhere near either pole.",,,10,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0015,53.22,56.98,"The closest road that qualifies is probably a long year being on the island of Svalbard, Norway.",,,17,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0016,56.98,59.5,The longest sunset there lasts just under an hour.,,,9,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0017,59.82,62.56,"In general, driving west to keep up with the sun isn't a viable strategy.",,,14,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0018,62.92,66.62,"Even at the northernmost tip of mainland Norway, you'd have to travel at about half the speed of",,,18,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0019,66.62,69.88,"sound to keep up with the sun. Luckily, there's a better approach.",,,12,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0020,70.18,74.14,"If you're in northern Scandinavia on a day when the sun just barely sets and then rises again,",,,18,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0021,74.4,79.58,"the day-night line moves northwest, then slows, reverses, and heads back to the southwest.",,,14,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0022,80.14,81.98,"To get along sunset, the strategy is simple.",,,8,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0023,82.32,86.72,"Sit in your car until the sun first touches the horizon, which means the day-night line is about to pass you,",,,21,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0024,86.72,89.94,"then drive north to stay a little ahead of the line as long as you can,",,,16,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0025,90.18,91.74,which will keep the sun in the process of setting.,,,10,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0026,92.0,95.16,Then you turn and drive south across the line in-night time.,,,11,,

+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0030,108.28,112.42,"consistently about 95 minutes, which is about 40 minutes longer than the longest sunset you can get",,,17,,
+how_long_could_you_drive_towards_the_sunset,S0031,112.42,116.62,"in Long-Year Bien. But if you are stuck on Svalbard and you want to make the sunset or sunrise,",,,19,,

+# Visual DNA
+
+## Global observed rules
+
+- **Character DNA — OBSERVED:** thin, black, hand-drawn stick figures; occasional red outline/speckled disintegration state. One presenter figure sometimes carries a paper or speaks via curved callout line.
+- **Environment DNA — OBSERVED:** sparse diagrammatic spaces: white paper-like fields, charcoal night fields, black silhouette ground, grey midtones. Buildings, machinery and props are ink outlines with deliberately uneven strokes.
+- **Object DNA — OBSERVED:** simple, high-contrast technical icons; many have no shading beyond grey fill. Nuclear/cesium items add cyan emission; failures use red detail.
+- **Palette — OBSERVED:** near-white, black, cool greys; red is alert/disappearance/accent; cyan is radioactive/energy glow; end card is flat red with black and white.
+- **Lighting — OBSERVED:** localized soft white pools for lamps and night scenes. Industrial daytime frames are flat white. Cyan objects have a soft outer glow. No photorealistic lighting.
+- **Camera/framing — OBSERVED:** locked orthographic-like 2D view. No evidence of camera pan, dolly, perspective parallax, or lens behavior. Reframing occurs by hard cut or a graphic wipe/slide.
+- **Composition — OBSERVED:** left-to-right explanatory staging; large negative space around diagrams; panels divide comparisons. Text is placed in clear unused space, usually top or center.
+- **Typography — OBSERVED:** hand-lettered, black, mostly all caps. Exact font unknown. Exact readable labels should be editor text, not image-generated text.
+- **Graphics — OBSERVED:** black callout lines, speech lines, warning symbols, panel borders, simple graphs and white/grey cards.
+- **Depth/style — OBSERVED:** flat 2D line illustration with silhouette layers; no observable 3D material or depth-of-field.
+- **Motion language — OBSERVED:** sparse sequential substitutions: lights extinguish, people convert to red particles, icons/cards appear, panels reveal, decay texture grows, rain overlays, and a final object splits. Static holds dominate.
+- **Transition language — OBSERVED:** hard cuts dominate. Some darken/fade-to-black, lateral reveal/slide, and simple element pop-ins occur. No evidence of decorative motion between every state.
+- **Reuse — LIKELY:** recurring visual vocabulary (same stick figures, pylon, wind turbine, lamp glow, warning signs, handwritten text treatment) is reused, but source files are UNKNOWN.
+
+## Scene exceptions
+
+- S02 and S26 are branded red cards, not part of normal monochrome explanatory field.
+- S19 uses concentric rings behind a large wristwatch; S21–S25 add cyan energy/radiation glow.
+- S16 uses a richer night roadside environment and rain overlay; camera stays locked.
+
+## Reconstruction constraints
+
+Use 24 fps, 16:9, locked framing, hand-drawn black outlines and off-white/grey fields. Red and cyan only where timeline assigns them. No global film grain, camera shake, parallax, bounce, or ambient particles. Any live texture in rain/disintegration must be limited to its assigned A-ID.

+[00.000–02.200]
+
+"This question comes from Alan who asks,"
+
+[02.720–05.540]
+
+"if every human somehow simply disappeared from the face of the Earth,"
+
+[05.760–08.600]
+
+"how long would it be before the last artificial light source would go out?"
+
+[10.440–11.620]
+
+"We'll start with the obvious."
+
+[12.020–15.520]
+
+"Most lights wouldn't last long because the major power grids would go down relatively quickly."
+
+[15.880–17.740]
+
+"Without people, there would be less demand for power,"
+
+[17.840–20.400]
+
+"but our fridges and air conditioners and lava lamps would still be running."
+
+[20.700–23.680]
+
+"Fossil fuel plants, which supply the vast majority of the world's electricity,"
+
+[23.980–25.180]
+
+"require a steady supply of fuel,"
+
+[25.360–27.760]
+
+"and their supply chains do involve people doing things."
+
+[27.760–30.720]
+
+"As coal and oil plants started shutting down in the first few hours,"
+
+[30.940–32.980]
+
+"other power sources would get hit with that extra load."
+
+[33.300–35.940]
+
+"This kind of situation is difficult to handle even with human guidance,"
+
+[36.200–38.500]
+
+"and the result would be a rapid series of cascading failures"
+
+[38.500–40.540]
+
+"leading to a blackout of all the major power grids."
+
+[41.060–43.900]
+
+"Nuclear reactors, of course, don't require a steady supply of fuel."
+
+[44.220–47.460]
+
+"One reactor operator I talked to said that if their cores settled into low power mode,"
+
+[47.580–49.380]
+
+"it could get any running almost indefinitely."
+
+[49.700–54.480]
+
+"A cube of uranium contains about 6 million times as much stored energy as a similar-sized cube of coal."
+
+[54.900–56.520]
+
+"Unfortunately, although there's enough fuel,"
+
+[56.940–58.900]
+
+"most nuclear reactors wouldn't keep running for long."
+
+[59.320–61.820]
+
+"As soon as something went wrong, the core would go into automatic shutdown."
+
+[62.280–66.500]
+
+"Every part of a reactor control system is designed so that a failure causes it to rapidly shut down."
+
+[66.880–67.620]
+
+"This would happen quickly."
+
+[67.960–71.900]
+
+"Many things can trigger a shutdown, but the most likely culprit would be the failure of the power grid."
+
+[72.340–75.840]
+
+"However, plenty of light comes from sources not tied to the major power grids."
+
+[76.120–78.480]
+
+"Let's take a look at a few of those and when each one might turn off."
+
+[78.880–82.860]
+
+"Many remote communities, like those on Far-Floong Islands, get their power from diesel generators."
+
+[82.860–87.420]
+
+"These can run until their tanks run out of fuel, which in most cases could be anywhere from days to months."
+
+[87.820–91.840]
+
+"Off-grid generating stations that don't need a human-provided fuel supply would be in better shape."
+
+[92.340–95.280]
+
+"Geothermal plants can run for a fair bit of time without human intervention."
+
+[95.740–99.020]
+
+"According to the maintenance schedule for the Sfartsangu Island Geothermal Plan in Iceland,"
+
+[99.400–103.760]
+
+"every six months the operators must change the gearbox oil and re-grease all electric motors and couplings."
+
+[104.160–106.240]
+
+"Without humans to perform these sorts of maintenance procedures,"
+
+[106.520–109.740]
+
+"some plants might run for a few years, but they'd also come to corrosion eventually."
+
+[110.220–112.320]
+
+"Lights relying on wind power would last a bit longer."
+
+[112.320–116.020]
+
+"Wind turbines are designed so that they don't need constant maintenance for the simple reason"
+
+[116.020–117.980]
+
+"that there are a lot of them and there are pain to climb."
+
+[118.440–123.660]
+
+"The Geitzer Wind turbine in Denmark was installed in the late 1950s and it generated power for 11 years without maintenance."
+
+[124.240–129.360]
+
+"Modern turbines are typically rated to run for three years without servicing and there are no doubt some which would run for decades."
+
+[129.780–132.500]
+
+"And one of them would probably have at least a status LED in it somewhere."
+
+[133.000–136.540]
+
+"Eventually, most of the wind turbines would be stopped by the same thing that would destroy the geothermal plants."
+
+[136.920–138.240]
+
+"Their gearboxes would seize up."
+
+[138.700–141.900]
+
+"Generates the convert-falling water into electricity will also keep working."
+
+[142.280–147.720]
+
+"An operator at the Hoover Dam once said that if everyone walked out, the facility would continue to run on autopilot for several years."
+
+[148.120–150.900]
+
+"Though if the power grid is down, all that electricity would have nowhere to go."
+
+[151.300–157.720]
+
+"In the end, the dam would probably succumb to clogged in-takes or the same kind of mechanical failure that hit the wind turbines and geothermal plants."
+
+[158.040–161.800]
+
+"Battery-powered lights wouldn't fare much better and would all be off within a few dozen years."
+
+[162.200–165.460]
+
+"Even without anything using their power, batteries eventually self-discharge."
+
+[165.460–171.720]
+
+"Some types last longer than others, but even batteries advertise as having long shelf-lives typically only hold their charge for a decade or two."
+
+[172.340–174.660]
+
+"Solar power is probably the most promising candidate."
+
+[175.100–179.820]
+
+"There are many off-grid solar-powered buildings, weather stations, and other remote infrastructure around the world."
+
+[180.120–184.440]
+
+"Emergency call boxes often found along the side of the road and remote locations are frequently solar-powered."
+
+[184.700–187.320]
+
+"They usually have lights on them which provide illumination every night."
+
+[187.680–190.780]
+
+"Like wind turbines, they're hard to service and so they're built to last for a long time."
+
+[190.780–197.060]
+
+"Solar panels will generally last as long as the electronics are connected to them and as long as the panels are kept free of dust and debris."
+
+[197.600–209.220]
+
+"The wires and circuits will eventually succumb to corrosion, but solar panels in a dry place with well-built electronics could easily continue providing power for a century if they're kept free of dust by occasional breezes or rain on the exposed panels."
+
+[209.700–216.100]
+
+"If we follow a strict definition of lighting, solar-powered lights and remote locations could conceivably be the last surviving human light source."
+
+[216.580–218.800]
+
+"But there's another contender and it's a weird one."
+
+[218.800–220.260]
+
+"Spent nuclear fuel."
+
+[220.700–227.440]
+
+"Contrary to popular portrayals, radioactivity isn't usually visible, which is part of why we need warning signs around areas with radioactive materials are waste."
+
+[227.980–234.340]
+
+"Sure, watchtiles used to be coated in small ions of radium to help them glow in the dark, but the glow didn't come from the radioactivity itself."
+
+[234.720–238.560]
+
+"It came from the phosphorous and paint on top of the radium, which glow is when it's irradiated."
+
+[239.000–243.020]
+
+"Once the phosphorous and paint breaks down, the watchtiles are still radioactive but no longer glow."
+
+[243.620–246.260]
+
+"Watchtiles, however, are not our only radioactive light source."
+
+[246.260–251.620]
+
+"When radioactive particles travel through materials like water or glass, they emit light through a sort of optical sonic boom."
+
+[252.060–256.720]
+
+"This light is called Cherenkov radiation and it's seen in the distinctive blue glow of nuclear reactor cores."
+
+[257.000–265.680]
+
+"Some of our radioactive waste products, such as CZM-137, are melted and mixed with glass, which cools into a solid block before being wrapped in more shielding for transport and storage."
+
+[266.160–268.640]
+
+"And in the dark, these glass blocks glow blue."
+
+[269.280–276.720]
+
+"CZM-137 has a half-life of 30 years, which means that two centuries later, the blocks will still be glowing with 1% of their original radioactivity."
+
+[277.020–281.440]
+
+"Since the color of the light depends only on the particle decay energy and not the amount of radiation,"
+
+[281.880–284.820]
+
+"it will fade in brightness over time, but keep that same blue color."
+
+[285.300–286.580]
+
+"And thus, we arrive at our answer."
+
+[287.000–292.020]
+
+"Centuries from now, deep and concrete vaults, the light from our most toxic waste will still be shining."
+

+if_all_humans_died,S0056,197.6,209.22,"The wires and circuits will eventually succumb to corrosion, but solar panels in a dry place with well-built electronics could easily continue providing power for a century if they're kept free of dust by occasional breezes or rain on the exposed panels.",,,42,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0057,209.7,216.1,"If we follow a strict definition of lighting, solar-powered lights and remote locations could conceivably be the last surviving human light source.",,,22,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0058,216.58,218.8,But there's another contender and it's a weird one.,,,9,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0059,218.8,220.26,Spent nuclear fuel.,,,3,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0060,220.7,227.44,"Contrary to popular portrayals, radioactivity isn't usually visible, which is part of why we need warning signs around areas with radioactive materials are waste.",,,24,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0061,227.98,234.34,"Sure, watchtiles used to be coated in small ions of radium to help them glow in the dark, but the glow didn't come from the radioactivity itself.",,,27,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0062,234.72,238.56,"It came from the phosphorous and paint on top of the radium, which glow is when it's irradiated.",,,18,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0063,239.0,243.02,"Once the phosphorous and paint breaks down, the watchtiles are still radioactive but no longer glow.",,,16,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0064,243.62,246.26,"Watchtiles, however, are not our only radioactive light source.",,,9,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0065,246.26,251.62,"When radioactive particles travel through materials like water or glass, they emit light through a sort of optical sonic boom.",,,20,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0066,252.06,256.72,This light is called Cherenkov radiation and it's seen in the distinctive blue glow of nuclear reactor cores.,,,18,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0067,257.0,265.68,"Some of our radioactive waste products, such as CZM-137, are melted and mixed with glass, which cools into a solid block before being wrapped in more shielding for transport and storage.",,,31,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0068,266.16,268.64,"And in the dark, these glass blocks glow blue.",,,9,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0069,269.28,276.72,"CZM-137 has a half-life of 30 years, which means that two centuries later, the blocks will still be glowing with 1% of their original radioactivity.",,,25,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0070,277.02,281.44,"Since the color of the light depends only on the particle decay energy and not the amount of radiation,",,,19,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0071,281.88,284.82,"it will fade in brightness over time, but keep that same blue color.",,,13,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0072,285.3,286.58,"And thus, we arrive at our answer.",,,7,,
+if_all_humans_died,S0073,287.0,292.02,"Centuries from now, deep and concrete vaults, the light from our most toxic waste will still be shining.",,,18,,

+# Visual DNA
+
+## Observed global rules
+
+- **Character DNA:** black-outline stick figures; circular heads; minimal facial detail. Some figures add black hair, beard, glasses, or a wrapped head.
+- **Environment DNA:** white paper-like field, sparse hand-drawn linework, thin black borders; scenes replace rather than share a literal continuous room.
+- **Object DNA:** simplified black-outline appliances and props. Toaster red/orange glow is repeated visual shorthand for heat.
+- **Palette / lighting:** near-white background, black line art, restrained red accent. Outdoor scene uses a grey night wash; title/end card use flat red.
+- **Camera / composition:** locked, orthographic-looking wide compositions. Changes are primarily hard cuts or whole-frame replacements; no evidenced decorative camera drift.
+- **Typography / graphics:** irregular hand-drawn uppercase and handwritten labels; scientific annotations use thin black type with red arrows/heat lines.
+- **Depth:** flat 2D layers with rare soft red glow around hot appliances.
+- **Motion language:** draw-on/reveal, state replacement, pop-in, opacity fade, and very short object/character pose swaps. Static holds dominate.
+- **Transition language:** hard cuts, one early full-frame push/replacement, one fade-to-dark in outdoor scene, and red bumper/end-card cuts.
+- **Asset reuse:** toaster, freezer/refrigerator motif, black-line character language, and red heat treatment recur across otherwise new plates.
+
+## Scene exceptions
+
+- S03 and S12 use branded red graphic cards rather than white line-art scenes.
+- S10 is grey night exterior; its red toaster remains chromatic focal point.
+- S08 is technical cutaway/diagram rather than character narrative.
+
+## Evidence limits
+
+Exact font, production software, original drawing source, music identity, and easing curves are UNKNOWN.

+[00.000–03.340]
+
+"I heard this question debated on a podcast I listened to, which asked,"
+
+[03.660–05.300]
+
+"would a toaster still work in a freezer?"
+
+[05.760–08.680]
+
+"Here's how they summed up the situation. You put a toaster in a freezer,"
+
+[08.960–12.120]
+
+"you put some bread in there, you click it down. What even happens, right?"
+
+[12.460–15.300]
+
+"Because if your answer is it would get hot, then the freezer hasn't done its job."
+
+[15.660–19.100]
+
+"But if you say it would get cold, then the toaster hasn't done its job."
+
+[19.540–22.480]
+
+"The answer is that the toaster would win, the freezer wouldn't do its job."
+
+[22.860–23.820]
+
+"Toaster's beat freezers."
+
+[24.240–28.940]
+
+"And less enough water melts inside the freezer to damage the toaster, in which case the circuit breaker might trip and shut down our experiment,"
+
+[28.940–30.220]
+
+"hopefully before anyone gets hurt."
+
+[32.220–36.600]
+
+"It's easy to think of a freezer and toaster as equivalent. One cools things down and the other warms them up."
+
+[36.900–39.780]
+
+"But toasters heat things up a lot more than freezers cool them down."
+
+[40.340–44.960]
+
+"The coils and regular toasters get hot enough to glow, which means they're over about 600 degrees Celsius."
+
+[45.520–47.280]
+
+"Since a toaster is operating at such high temperatures,"
+
+[47.500–52.720]
+
+"it would hardly notice whether the surrounding environment is 20 degrees C, 4 degrees C, or negative 15 degrees C."
+
+[52.980–56.560]
+
+"From a toaster's point of view, a 40 degree change in starting temperature hardly matters."
+
+[56.560–62.800]
+
+"As anyone has ever burned a piece of toaster nose, toasters are definitely capable of heating bread well above the ideal temperature for toast."
+
+[63.240–64.880]
+
+"But the black gasters had a follow-up question."
+
+[65.220–68.700]
+
+"If you left both the toaster and the freezer running, which would win in the long term?"
+
+[69.320–70.140]
+
+"It's still the toaster."
+
+[70.540–74.760]
+
+"A toaster produces about a thousand wants of heat, and a household freezer can't remove heat that fast."
+
+[75.160–78.740]
+
+"Refersers and freezers work by soaking up heat from their interior and dumping it out the back."
+
+[78.740–86.560]
+
+"Treasers have a coefficient of performance of two or three, which means it takes them one unit of electrical energy to move two or three units of heat energy from the interior to the exterior."
+
+[86.940–90.160]
+
+"A toaster, on the other hand, produces one unit of heat from one unit of electricity."
+
+[90.600–94.340]
+
+"So toaster is less efficient than a freezer, but it's far more powerful."
+
+[94.680–97.140]
+
+"A threase is compressor typically only draws a few hundred watts."
+
+[97.520–102.180]
+
+"So even with the efficiency multiplier, you can't keep up with the toaster's thousand plus watts of heat production."
+
+[102.480–105.120]
+
+"Eventually, the toaster will start to heat the inside of the freezer."
+
+[105.120–110.980]
+
+"And even if the freezer were as powerful as the toaster, it wouldn't be able to keep the toaster coils themselves from getting hot and toasting bread."
+
+[111.280–115.800]
+
+"The freezer can make the air around the toaster cold, but remember to the toaster all our air is cold."
+
+[116.440–119.960]
+
+"If you happen to live in the Canadian city of Winnipeg, you can check this experimentally."
+
+[120.240–126.700]
+
+"The winter night time temperature in Winnipeg is about the same as the inside of a freezer, so it simulates a freezer with infinite capacity to absorb heat."
+
+[127.140–132.880]
+
+"Suppose you put a toaster out on your portion Winnipeg and left it running for a few hours, going outside every so often to collect the toast and put in fresh bread."
+
+[132.880–133.780]
+
+"What would happen?"
+
+[134.280–136.060]
+
+"Simple. You'd quickly be eaten by wolves."
+
+[136.580–141.280]
+
+"But assuming you survived the experiment, you should find that the toaster doesn't have trouble working in the cold air."
+
+[141.600–147.160]
+
+"It might take a bit longer to get the bread properly browned, but unless the wind is extremely strong, it should be able to manage it fine."
+
+[147.580–150.120]
+
+"After all, to a toaster, all weather is cold."
+
